prize_parts.citation: for visionary, densely patterned Romanian-language prose in which memory, the body and dream are built into a metaphysical architecture of exceptional scale and unmistakable voice, across a long oeuvre

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one prize part, B007, with Mircea Cărtărescu as the single credited name. The round-1 exchange did not weaken the literary case, but it did sharpen what a citation can honestly claim. The case rests on a voice I find in this writer's work and nowhere else, on a formal and linguistic ambition sustained at very large scale, and on imaginative depth. From public knowledge, Blinding (the first volume of the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid turn memory, the body, dream and metaphysical speculation into one project. Attribution is clean, with one author and one principal language. I have narrowed the citation. It is anchored in the prose, and the demonstrated peak is the Orbitor trilogy and Solenoid. I would name poetry and essays only if a colleague can attest to them from direct reading of the Romanian. The chair's summary notes that every member's knowledge of the poetry is thin, and a citation should not claim more than has been assessed. The unanimity of the openings is not a merit argument, and I do not rely on it. The question the chair posed is whether this case survives the strongest alternatives, and I think it does, though not by default. It is the case I can best weigh on the evidence available to me, even though that evidence is translation and public reception, not a full reading.
statement.case_against: The most serious reservation is unresolved. I do not know whether Solenoid and the later large novels deepen the project or repeat its method. I cannot settle that from translated reception, and no colleague has claimed a book-level reading that settles it. A second reservation is that density and encyclopedic excess may be imaginatively necessary in one book and merely mannered in another. A third is that the Romanian rhythm and syntax, which are central to the linguistic achievement, are the least verifiable part of my judgment. Adonis's renewal of a whole poetic language is a serious competing claim, and my low opening rank for him (sixth) reflected my own lack of access to Arabic prosody, not a settled literary judgment. If a colleague with direct Arabic competence were to show that the later poetry sustains the foundational books, I would weigh that case much more closely against Cărtărescu's. Zurita's printed sequences remain a serious alternative if they carry the case without the landscape-scale works.

responses.point: Olsson says the repetition question cannot be settled by pointing to scale, and that Solenoid and the later work must be shown to transform the motifs and not only repeat them. He would rest the citation on the poetry and novels together and treat the poetry as a test of the oeuvre's unity.
responses.response: I agree that scale does not answer the repetition question, and I accept the test he proposes: do the later books transform the motifs of memory, body and cosmos, or only restate them? I differ on the poetry. As a test of unity it is a good idea, but a test needs a reader who has actually done it. Nobody in round 1 claims to have assessed the poetry, and I include myself. So I would not name poetry in the citation on the strength of its presence in the ballot entry. I would anchor the citation in the prose, say 'across a long oeuvre', and add poetry only if someone can report a direct reading. This changes my citation wording from round 1, not my preferred laureate.

responses.point: Sward ranks Adonis second and would keep him as her first alternative because the formal case looks strong even through partial translation. She also notes that her citation names prose only, and that longevity does not guarantee sustained quality, which applies to her own preferred candidate as well.
responses.response: Her point that longevity cuts both ways is fair, and it is why I do not want to use age or timing against Adonis or for Cărtărescu. I also take her prose-only citation as a model for scope. Her argument for Adonis has moved me to treat him as the strongest competing case. My own opening ranked him sixth, but I based that on limited access to the Arabic, not on a judgment of the work. I have therefore replaced Robinson with Adonis among my alternatives. I still cannot test her claim that the formal case holds through partial translation, since prosody and sound are exactly what translation loses. The committee should compare the foundational books with the later poetry, and I would defer to a reader of Arabic on that comparison.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg reads the recurrence of obsessions (body, memory, dream, cosmology) as the project's method, which deepens across the major novels. He also says translation lowers confidence about Adonis's prosody but not the documented scale of his reshaping of Arabic poetic language.
responses.response: I share his reading of recurrence as method, but I hold it as a hypothesis, as he does, not as a finding. The distinction I would apply is whether each major novel adds a new formal or imaginative move or only widens the same one. On Adonis, I think his distinction between confidence about prosody and the documented scale of the renewal is useful, and I am persuaded that the translation problem should not lead the committee to rank him low by default. It lowers how securely we can judge his diction and metre. It does not remove his historical transformation of the language from the comparison. I would still hold that it makes my own preference for Cărtărescu provisional, not that it overturns it.

responses.point: Carlberg agrees that recurrence is a flaw only if the later books repeat the method without adding to it. She would frame the citation around the Orbitor trilogy and Solenoid as the demonstrated peak, not around the whole corpus equally, and asks whether the committee has reliable Romanian-language readings of the later volumes.
responses.response: I agree with this framing and have adopted it. The citation should claim the demonstrated peak and say nothing about the whole corpus that the committee has not assessed. Her question about reliable Romanian-language readings is the practical one, and I cannot answer it from my own evidence. I would add that if no such readings exist within the committee, the uncertainty belongs in the recommendation's record and not in a stronger-sounding citation. On the same evidentiary standard, Zurita and Adonis face their own gaps in Spanish and Arabic, so the unequal translation limits you and the chair describe should be recorded as unequal, not resolved in favor of whichever case is easiest to read.

responses.point: Palm reads the density as disciplined by recurring structures and images, not as simple accumulation, while accepting that recurrence is a hypothesis. She says she would want the committee to read what exists of the poetry before crediting it.
responses.response: I agree on the poetry and have drawn the same consequence for the citation. On density, I agree that disciplined recurrence and accumulation are different things and that the committee needs a criterion to tell them apart. A workable one is whether a passage or book could be removed without loss to the architecture, or whether the same image returns without a new relation to the whole. I cannot apply it without a full reading, so I offer it as a question for those who have read more closely. I also note that her willingness to keep Adonis as an alternative despite her weakest access to the Arabic is a sound way to handle unequal limits.

uncertainties: How much of the Romanian rhythm, syntax and density survives in the translations I know, and whether those translations are representative.
Whether Solenoid and the later large novels deepen the project or repeat its method. No colleague has reported a book-level reading that settles this, and I have not made one.
The poetry, early prose and essays are thinly covered, so I have kept the citation prose-anchored. Whether a whole-oeuvre citation can responsibly name them is unresolved.

Adonis: the committee's competence in Arabic prosody is uncertain, and I do not know how the later poetry compares with the foundational books. My low opening rank for him was based on limited access, not a literary judgment.
Zurita: whether the printed sequences carry the case without the landscape-scale works, and how much incantatory rhythm survives translation from Spanish.

I have not independently verified sources or read the corpora for this exercise. My assessments rest on public knowledge and translated reception, and the six-member count, including a co-opted member whose voting status is undocumented, is a modeling assumption.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any shortlisted writer is apparent from the supplied profile, and the profile records no tie to any of them. I am a novelist, and my published work includes a dream-logic novel (Den svarta månens år, 2021). I treat my own practice as context and not as evidence that I favor Cărtărescu or any other candidate, and I note that this overlap in manner could be mistaken for a preference. My ties to committee colleagues are ordinary professional ones. This disclosure is recorded and not adjudicated.
